periods.activity_title: Reading and Exploring the Farmer's Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (pp.78–81): shared reading of the story with mid-point prediction.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story 'Thank God!' aloud from pp.78–81 while students follow in their textbooks. Teacher pauses at the mid-point illustration to let students notice details — the king throwing grapes, the farmer's expression — before reading on.

Let us read (pp.78–81) — shared reading with prediction. Students take turns reading a paragraph each. At p.79, teacher poses the prediction prompt: 'What do you think will happen next?' Students share their guesses aloud briefly before reading continues.

Let us think — A. (pp.82) — comprehension discussion of questions 1–5. Teacher reads each question aloud; students think quietly for a moment, then partners share their answers before two or three pairs report to the class.

Class draws together by retelling the story's turning point in a single sentence: why the farmer said 'Thank God!' Teacher takes three to four responses and affirms the theme — wisdom in choosing what fits the situation.

periods.teacher_notes: The farmer's logic — grapes are lighter than watermelons, so grapes were the wiser gift — is the story's comic and moral hinge; give students time to appreciate the humour before drawing out the wisdom. Students often miss that the farmer's relief is genuine gratitude, not sarcasm — a quick re-reading of his explanation on p.81 helps. Question 5 ('Why did the farmer say Thank God?') is the richest comprehension moment; prompt students to use the farmer's own reasoning in their answer.

periods.activity_title: Speaking, Listening, and the Elephant's Cold

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B. (p.82): guided discussion on farmers and their work.
Let us speak (p.86): say aloud which foods you'd bring a sick elephant.
Let us listen (p.85): teacher reads 'Aachoo!' poem; students listen and respond.

time_bands.activity: Let us think — B. (p.82) — guided conversation on farming. Teacher poses the three prompts one at a time: what else can farmers grow, are there women farmers, and what would you say to a farmer. Students discuss in pairs; each pair shares one idea with the class.

Let us listen (p.85) — teacher reads the poem 'Aachoo!' aloud slowly, three times. Students listen with books closed. After the second reading, teacher invites them to join in on the 'AACHOO!' line. After the third, students describe what they pictured — the elephant, the shop, the salesperson's surprise.

Let us speak (p.86) — students look at the illustration of the sick elephant wrapped in a scarf. Teacher sets the scene: 'You are visiting this elephant. What food items will you bring?' Students say their choices aloud one by one, using a simple frame: 'I will bring _____ because _____.' Three or four students share.

Brief whole-class share-out: teacher asks which food the class thinks would most help the elephant and why. Students vote with a show of hands and give a one-sentence reason, tying back to the fruits the farmer grew in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem 'Aachoo!' (p.85) rewards repeated listening — the comic logic of the elephant needing a whole sheet mirrors the story's wisdom about matching size to situation. For the speaking task, students who are shy may simply name a fruit; the 'because' clause is an extension, not a requirement. Linking the elephant's food choices back to the farmer's fruits keeps both activities in the same imaginative world.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.86): sequence the mixed-up fruit salad steps in correct order.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the task by reading all seven of Chandu's fruit-salad slips aloud in their mixed-up order (p.86). Students notice the slips use sequencing words — 'First', 'Next', 'Then', 'After that', 'Finally' — and teacher lists them on the board as anchors for ordering.

Teacher models ordering the first two slips: 'Mother cuts some fruits for me' must come early because you need cut fruit before anything else; 'First I take some banana slices' signals the opening action. Students decide aloud where each of the remaining slips belongs, with teacher guiding discussion rather than confirming answers immediately.

Let us write (p.86) — students number the seven slips in their textbooks independently. Teacher circulates, asking individual students to read their ordering aloud and explain their reasoning using the sequence words. Partners compare their numbering and resolve any differences by referring to the sequence clues in the slip texts.

Class confirms the correct order together: teacher calls on volunteers to read each slip in sequence until the full recipe is spoken aloud in order. Teacher draws out that sequencing words helped — the same skill that makes a recipe clear makes a story clear.

periods.teacher_notes: The correct order is: Mother cuts fruits → First banana slices → Next papaya cubes → Then apple slices → After that grapes → Then mix them all → Finally lemon and salt. Students often place the lemon-and-salt step too early; direct attention to 'Finally' as the decisive clue. The activity connects naturally to the fruits the farmer grew — banana, papaya, grapes all appear in both the story and the salad.

periods.activity_title: Opposites and Is / Are in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A. (p.83): write the opposite of the underlined word in each phrase.
Let us learn — B. and C. (p.84): understand is/are and fill in the blanks.

time_bands.activity: Let us learn — A. (p.83) — opposites from the story. Teacher recalls aloud that the farmer called watermelons heavy and grapes light. 'Heavy' and 'light' are opposites. Teacher reads the four phrases (thick book, long journey, soft cotton, slow tortoise) and students call out their opposite word for each, with teacher confirming and writing the pairs on the board.

Students write the four opposite-word answers in their textbooks (p.83). Teacher circulates and draws attention to meaning: 'Why can't we say a "heavy" book is "small"?' — guiding students to see that opposites must match the same quality being described.

Let us learn — B. and C. (p.84) — singular/plural and is/are in context. Teacher reads the two example sentences ('The ball is round'; 'The tables are brown') and asks students what changes — one ball, many tables. Students then complete all eight fill-in-the-blank sentences (p.84) independently in their textbooks.

Partners swap textbooks and check each other's is/are answers. Teacher reads the correct answers aloud; students self-correct. Teacher closes by asking students to make up one new sentence using 'are' about something in the classroom, connecting grammar to the room around them.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'are' for singular nouns that feel important or large ('Raghuram are a tall boy') — return to the example sentences on p.84 and have students count: one person, one thing → 'is'. The opposite-word activity anchors the vocabulary in the story's own language (heavy/light) before moving to new pairs, which helps students see that they already know the concept. All eight is/are blanks can be managed in a single sitting at this pace.

periods.activity_title: Fruit Word Search and Vocabulary Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore — A. (p.87): find eight fruit words in the 8×8 word search grid.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the eight target fruit words aloud — MANGO, PAPAYA, GRAPES, BANANA, GUAVA, PLUM, PEACH, PEAR — and students repeat each one. Teacher asks which of these fruits appeared in the farmer's story and which were in Chandu's salad, briefly connecting the word list to the chapter's fruit-rich world.

Let us explore — A. (p.87) — students open to the 8×8 word search grid. Teacher explains that words can run horizontally or vertically. Students work individually to find and circle all eight fruit words, calling out 'found one!' quietly when they locate a word. Teacher circulates, pointing quieter students toward the grid's edges where shorter words (PLUM, PEAR) often hide.

Teacher leads a whole-class check: for each of the eight words, one student says the row or column they found it in and teacher confirms. Any word not yet found is located together as a class. Students who finished early write each found word in a sentence of their own on the back of their notebook page.

Closing vocabulary round: teacher points to each fruit word on the board and students call out one fact or association — colour, taste, shape, or where it grows. The unit ends with a brief appreciative reference to the farmer who grew many of these same fruits and whose wise choice is the heart of the chapter's story.

periods.teacher_notes: PAPAYA and BANANA are the longest words in the grid and usually the last to be found — if students are stuck after a good search, suggest scanning column by column rather than row by row. The word search works best as a focused individual task followed by a communal check; resist the urge to confirm answers too early. The sentence-writing extension for early finishers (using each fruit word) keeps the activity connected to the writing and word-work the chapter has already practised.

items.source_lo: Student infers character motivation and draws meaning from key story events using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Farmer gifts grapes to king; king throws grapes; farmer explains grateful hindsight about watermelons.
items.item_stem: Why did the farmer choose to bring grapes to the king instead of watermelons?

options.label: A
options.text: The king had asked specifically for grapes.

options.label: B
options.text: Grapes were lighter and easier to carry on the long journey.

options.label: C
options.text: The watermelons on the farm were not yet ripe.

options.label: D
options.text: His wife had already packed the grapes for him.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have inferred that the king's preference guided the gift, missing the farmer's own reasoning about weight.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have confused the ripeness detail — the story says the fruits were ripe and the finest; ripeness was not the issue.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have misremembered the wife's role; she pointed out the finest fruits but the farmer made the final choice himself.

items.source_lo: Student infers character motivation and draws meaning from key story events using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Farmer gifts grapes to king; king throws grapes; farmer explains grateful hindsight about watermelons.
items.item_stem: When the king threw grapes at the farmer one by one, the farmer said 'Thank God!' each time. In one to three sentences, explain what the farmer meant and why he was grateful in that moment.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The farmer was grateful because he had brought grapes instead of watermelons. If he had brought heavy watermelons and the king had thrown those, the farmer would have been badly hurt. He thanked God for inspiring the wise choice of bringing grapes.

items.source_context: Discussion on farming and farmers; listening to the 'Aachoo!' elephant poem; speaking task about food for a sick elephant.
items.item_stem: Listen carefully as your teacher reads the poem 'Aachoo!' aloud. Which of the following best describes what the elephant decided to do when it could not get a handkerchief?

options.label: A
options.text: It left the shop without buying anything.

options.label: B
options.text: It asked for a sheet instead of a handkerchief.

options.label: C
options.text: It sneezed so hard that the shop was blown away.

options.label: D
options.text: It asked the sales girl to make a bigger handkerchief.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may not have followed the poem to its final stanza, where the elephant makes a practical request.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have over-dramatised the 'AACHOO!' exclamation — the poem shows the sneeze as a reaction, not a destructive event.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have confused the elephant's request — it did not ask for a custom-made handkerchief but for a different item entirely.

items.item_stem:
Read the three steps below from Chandu's fruit salad recipe. They are in the wrong order. Write the number 1, 2 or 3 in the box to show the correct order.
( ) Then I add the apple slices.
( ) First I take some banana slices.
( ) Next, I put in papaya cubes.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — First I take some banana slices. 2 — Next, I put in papaya cubes. 3 — Then I add the apple slices.

items.item_stem: Think of something you do every morning — like washing your face, eating breakfast, or packing your bag. Write two to three sentences describing the steps in the correct order. Use words like 'First', 'Then', and 'Finally' to show the sequence.

expected_elements: Uses at least two sequencing words correctly.
Steps are in a logical, believable order.
